analysis.one_liner: Gradually cuts interest rates on federal undergraduate student loans from 6.8% to 3.4%.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lowered the fixed interest rate that undergraduate students pay on subsidized federal student loans, stepping it down from 6.8% each year until it reached 3.4% in July 2011. It was introduced in January 2007 by Senator Richard Durbin, sent to the Senate's education committee, and was never taken up. No vote was ever held on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Undergraduate students borrowing subsidized federal student loans would pay less interest over the life of their loans, saving money for years after graduation.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the interest rate on subsidized undergraduate loans in steps from 6.8% to 6.12% in July 2007, then down each year to 5.44%, 4.76%, 4.08%, and finally 3.4% by July 2011.
Applies to loans made, insured, or guaranteed under the Federal Family Education Loan program, the main federal student loan channel at the time.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, because lower interest payments from borrowers under the government-guaranteed loan system mean larger federal subsidy payments to keep lenders whole.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no funding mechanism; because the loans were government-guaranteed, the cost of the rate cut would show up as larger federal subsidy payments rather than as a loss borne by the loan industry.
The rate cut applied only to future loans (based on when the first disbursement was made), so students with existing loans got no relief from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A real and meaningful benefit to student borrowers, paid for by the federal budget rather than by the lending industry, which kept its guaranteed role in the loan system. The design shifted the cost to taxpayers, but the underlying policy was widely popular and, in fact, was enacted that same year through a separate, larger education law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate education committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it, so it died quietly when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Durbin introduced the bill in the Senate on January 12, 2007, with Senator Edward Kennedy as its one cosponsor.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
The bill would have phased in a reduction of the subsidized undergraduate loan interest rate from 6.8% to 3.4% over five years.
No further action was ever recorded; the committee never took it up and it never reached the Senate floor before the 110th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed through this bill. Students ultimately received the same 3.4% rate cut anyway through a separate education law enacted later in 2007, so borrowers were not harmed by this bill's death, and the student loan industry's guaranteed role was untouched by this route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The loan industry; students were covered elsewhere

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut subsidized undergraduate loan interest rates to 3.4% over five years.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 12, 2007 and never reported it out or scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators appear on the record — the sponsor and one cosponsor — with no Republican positions recorded and no votes taken, so no partisan pattern can be established.

industries.industry: Student loan lenders and guarantors (FFEL industry)
industries.note: The bill cut the interest rate students pay on government-guaranteed FFEL loans but left the guaranteed loan system itself intact, meaning taxpayers would make up the difference through federal subsidy payments to lenders. Lenders' protected, guaranteed role in federal student lending was preserved even as borrowers' rates fell.
Borrowers of subsidized undergraduate loans would have saved thousands of dollars in interest as rates stepped down to 3.4%.
